issues.legal_issue: A landlord who occupies a non-residential building that the landlord owns or is entitled to possess in the same locality cannot obtain possession of another non-residential building from a tenant for business purposes, regardless of the suitability or convenience of the building already occupied.
material_facts: The eviction petition sought a non-residential building for business use.
The landlord was already in possession of several shops and other buildings in the same locality.
issues.conclusion: The landlord’s occupation of another non-residential building that the landlord owned or was entitled to possess barred recovery of the tenanted building under the provision, and the suitability or convenience of the existing building was irrelevant. The Court also agreed that the bar does not apply where a landlord faces threatened eviction from premises the landlord occupies as a tenant.
issues.legal_principle: Section 10(3)(a)(iii) of the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act makes the landlord’s lack of occupation of another non-residential building that the landlord owns or is entitled to possess a condition for seeking possession. The Court agreed with Vidya Bai v. Shankerlal, which treated that bar as absolute where the landlord occupies such a building, and with Vijayalaxmi Printing Press v. Nandula Shankar, which recognized that threatened eviction from occupied tenanted premises does not bar an application and that the landlord need not first vacate those premises. It rejected the contrary interpretation in Balaiah v. Chandoor Lachaiah, distinguished J. Pandu v. R. Narsubai on its facts, and held that the cited Madras High Court decisions did not state the law correctly.

predicates.nonresidential_tenant_eviction_proceedin: A landlord sought to recover a non-residential building from a tenant for business use.
predicates.landlord_occupies_owned_or_possessable_b: The landlord occupied another non-residential building in the same locality that the landlord owned or was entitled to possess.
predicates.threatened_eviction_from_occupied_tenanc: The landlord occupied the other premises as a tenant and faced a threat of eviction from those premises.
predicates.recovery_of_another_business_premises_is: The landlord cannot recover another non-residential building from the tenant for business use.

issues.definition: When a landlord seeks a non-residential building for business use while occupying another owned or possessable business premises, the landlord cannot recover the additional building unless the occupied premises are tenanted and the landlord faces threatened eviction.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord’s asserted business requirement is not bona fide when the evidence shows that the landlord already has multiple business premises and an independent office, did not use the existing shops for the asserted purpose, and sought eviction after a dispute over increased rent.
material_facts: The landlord claimed to need the tenanted building, where a hotel business was operating, to store fire clay connected with a mining lease.
The landlord had eight shops in the same locality, an independent office, two houses, and another building in the town.
The landlord had not used any of the eight shops for storage.
The tenant’s evidence, corroborated by two mediators, was that the landlord demanded a substantial rent increase, refused the tenant’s lower proposed increase, and then sought eviction.
The appellate court found the claimed requirement not bona fide, but the High Court reversed that decision; the Supreme Court found the appellate court’s factual finding well-founded.
issues.conclusion: The landlord’s asserted business requirement was not bona fide. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court judgment, restored the appellate court’s decision, and rejected the eviction application.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 10(3)(a)(iii) of the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, the landlord must establish a bona fide requirement for the business being carried on or genuinely proposed. The appellate court’s assessment of the evidence showed that the asserted need was belied by the landlord’s existing premises and conduct; the High Court had not considered that evidence in its proper perspective.

predicates.claimed_business_requirement_is_not_bona: The landlord’s asserted need for the premises for business is not genuine.

issues.definition: In an appeal concerning eviction for business use, the asserted need is not genuine when the landlord has multiple existing business premises, has not used them for the claimed purpose, and sought eviction after a rent increase dispute.
